extracted.intended_audience: playwrights and poets (writers of serious/heroic drama)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing 'heroic plays' — serious verse dramas modeled on epic/heroic poetry emphasizing love and valour, elevated language, spectacle, and an expanded dramatic scale. Advice covers form (rhyme/verse), subject-matter, plot and character design, and permissible extraordinary or supernatural elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious plays should not imitate ordinary conversation too nearly
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the arguments which are formed against it, can amount to no more than this, that it is not so near conversation as prose, and therefore not so natural. But it is very clear to all who understand poetry, that serious plays ought not to imitate conversation too nearly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raise thoughts, images and actions above ordinary life; poetry's aim is to elevate rather than to reproduce common speech. Avoid making the verse merely conversational — the dramatic verse should possess an elevated dignity appropriate to heroic subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the heroic play on the heroic (epic) poem
rubrics_metrics.description: “An heroic play ought to be an imitation, in little, of an heroic poem; and, consequently, that love and valour ought to be the subject of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the drama as a condensed epic: central themes should be love and valor, and the play should aim for the grandeur, imagery and lofty purpose of epic poetry while remaining fit for the stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter: love and valour as primary themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted program from Ariosto: “Le donne, i cavalier, l'arme, gli amori” — love and arms (valour) should dominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make love and military/honor pursuits the main engines of action and character motivation. The heroic play's moral and emotional weight should derive from these twin concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain design, fullness of plot and variety of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of D'Avenant: there wanted “the fulness of a plot, and the variety of characters to form it as it ought.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write a mere narrated poem for the stage. Provide a well-formed plot, a sufficient cast of varied characters, and a variety of incidents and accidents to sustain theatrical interest and complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce the heroic play to a ‘play in narration’
rubrics_metrics.description: A work that is “rather a play in narration, as I may call it, than an heroic poem” fails by lacking theatrical persons and incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor enacted scenes and visible action over extended narrative summaries; exploit the stage's ability to show rather than tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme (heroic verse) is appropriate for serious/heroic plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense of rhyme: though it is not as near conversation, heroic verse is justified and should be used in serious plays; critics who write poorly in rhyme have dishonored it, not the form itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verse/rhyme to elevate tone and musicality, but respect craft — lazy or bad rhyming undermines the effect. Rhyme must carry sense as well as sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: The laws of the heroic poem raise rather than dispense with dramatic laws
rubrics_metrics.description: “The laws of an heroic poem did not dispense with those of the other [drama], but raised them to a greater height, and indulged him a farther liberty of fancy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve essential dramatic principles (coherent action, unity where appropriate) but allow amplified style, larger incidents and freer imagination consistent with epic grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (drums, trumpets, battles) is necessary to produce heroic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of warlike instruments and the presentation of battles are defended as necessary to raise the imagination and persuade the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ stage music, martial effects and battle-scenes (or their convincing representation) to create the appropriate heroic atmosphere and to make the audience feel the magnitude of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow visionary, supernatural, and magical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may 'let themselves loose to visionary objects' — gods, spirits, spectres and magical palaces are legitimate parts of heroic poetry and play: examples cited (Polydorus' ghost, Enchanted Wood, Bower of Bliss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject spectres or magic on grounds of improbability alone; such elements can enrich imagery and thematic depth. Ensure they fit the poem's imaginative law and contribute to its nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry can better explicate metaphysical/visionary problems than philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: On separated beings: 'may better be explicated by poets than by philosophers or divines' — poets' fancy is fit for such subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with spirits or metaphysical matters, embrace poetic explanation and imagery rather than pedantic philosophical treatment; use imaginative coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic characters may have noble imperfections (eccentric virtues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes need not be morally flawless: 'a character of an eccentrick virtue is the more exact image of human life... such a person is Almanzor... roughness of character, impatient of injuries, and a confidence of himself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give heroes grand, sometimes excessive qualities (overbearing courage, pride, intense passion) so long as they remain heroic at core and those imperfections humanize rather than flatten them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unmotivated bombast and extravagant egotism in heroic speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Overweening vaunts and ranting that have no credible motivation are defects (example: passages of Almanzor are called 'bombastic' and 'extravagant egotism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevated language must still suit character and situation; passion should illuminate character or plot, not merely produce empty boastfulness. Keep rhetoric credible within the heroic temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance rapid changes of fortune with plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'changes of fortune are too rapid to be either probable, or altogether pleasing', they can still arrest attention by their splendour and importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatic reversals and rapid events for spectacle, but avoid so many or such abrupt turns that the plot loses plausibility or emotional weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use well-managed underplots to enrich the main action
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'under plot of the loves of Ozmyn and Benzayda is beautiful in itself, and ingeniously managed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include subplots (romantic or domestic) that provide contrast, human interest, and emotional depth, and that are deftly integrated with the heroic main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate characters and language with appropriate locality and patriotic motive when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that in a siege 'the principle of patriotism is hardly once alluded to' — absence of local or national feeling can be a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When historical or national stakes are central (e.g., sieges, wars), give the play local color, relevant allusions, and motives (patriotism, religion) to ground the heroics in recognizable stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit the stage's visual advantage over narration
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama 'represents to view what the poem only does relate; and, Segnius irritant animum demissa per aures, quam quae sunt oculis subjecta fidelibus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes that make powerful visual impressions; rely on enacted spectacle and stagecraft to move the audience more effectively than mere description.
